newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi banks post strong first-half results.
newsitem.headline: Saudi banks post strong first-half results.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's 12 commercial banks have notched up steady net profit growth this year, led by improved returns in local securities markets and higher customer deposits, bankers based in the kingdom said on Tuesday.

Net profits at the six Saudi banks that have announced first-half 1997 results so far rose by an average of 22.9 percent, ranging from 6.4 percent growth at Saudi American Bank to 56.6 percent at Saudi Investment Bank.

"Profit growth was on account of some very good share business, mutual funds did well and trade finance, together with interest from government bonds, were also strong," said a spokesman for Riyadh-based Saudi Hollandi Bank.

"Liquidity will be a little bit tighter in the second half of the year because oil prices have fallen but it (profit outlook for Saudi banks) does not look much different from the first half," the spokesman said.

First-half total net profit from Arab National Bank, Citicorp's joint venture Saudi American Bank, HSBC's Saudi British Bank, Saudi French Bank, Saudi Hollandi and Saudi Investment Bank totalled more than 1.4 billion Saudi riyals ($378 million).
Assets from the six banks that have published first-half results rose to $41.8 billion from $39.3 billion.

The improvement in earnings was despite a downturn in revenue from loans after higher oil prices in 1996 allowed the Saudi government to clear a back-log of heavy debts to contractors, suppliers and farmers, bankers said.
"The impact of higher liquidity in the Saudi economy resulted in slower loans and advances growth than expected," Saudi British Bank said in a statement with its results.

Only 12 banks are allowed to operate in the country which has a population of 18 million, one third of them foreigners. All foreign banks operate with Saudi joint venture partners. Interest rates paid on customer deposits are low or non-existent because of Islamic law and banks have an exclusive role in most aspects of the domestic capital market.
The number of banks operating in Saudi Arabia is expected to fall to 11 after an announcement by Riyadh-based United Saudi Commercial Bank that it would merge with Saudi Cairo Bank.

National Commercial Bank, the country's largest in terms of equity, saw first quarter profit rise to 267 million riyals from 223 million. Riyad Bank, the second largest in terms of assets, gained 5.6 percent in the same period to 238 million riyals.

Both banks and the Al-Rajhi Banking and Investment Corporation -- which has the largest number of branches in the country and operates according to Islamic law banning payment and receipt of interest -- are expected to release information on first-half performance over the coming month.

Saudi Arabia's stock market has risen by 6.5 percent since the start of the year though Saudi banks, which can execute share dealing only on behalf of clients rather than their own book, have also benefited from a surge in trading volume.

Trade volume on the exchange reached 126.3 million shares worth 21.3 billion riyals in the first six months of 1997 versus 53.3 million shares worth 9.2 billion riyals in the same period a year earlier. Market capitalisation has soared 22 percent.

The kingdom's central bank, the Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency (SAMA), first offered three- and five-year floating rate notes (FRNs) in December. Roughly 25 percent of Saudi bank deposits are held in bonds, analysts said.
